new_statements.quote: [p.84] In addition to the tones that operate at the syllable level, pitch in Turung speech is affected by two other considerations: stress, which is a phrase level phenomenon, and intonation, which is an utterance level phenomenon. ... Given the frequency of iambic (short-long) structures in this language, it is somewhat surprising that at the phrase level, stress appears to fall on the penultimate syllable, provided that syllable is not a minor syllable. [pp.199-200] This penultimate stress is analysed as applying to the penultimate major syllable. ... The minor syllable in the sesquisyllable is not counted when calculating the penultimate syllable on which stress will fall. The syllabic nasal is also not counted when assigning stress to the penultimate

new_statements.rule_in_words: Turung (Singpho variety) has three lexical tones on major syllables; words are frequently sesquisyllabic/iambic, the minor (schwa) syllable being unstressed and toneless (p.98; Morey 2014:651 'strongly iambic, with stress on final syllables'). Stress proper is analysed as a phrase-level phenomenon: within a phrase (including compounds, noun + definiteness marker, and verb complexes) stress falls on the penultimate MAJOR syllable, skipping minor syllables and syllabic nasals; because disyllables may reduce to sesquisyllables the stressed syllable can surface as the antepenultimate written syllable (p.200). The author flags the stress-tone interaction as needing much more analysis (p.84).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Only relative weakness of minor syllables, light verbs and particles versus the stressed penultimate element is discussed (pp.199-201, 493-494).
new_statements.exceptions: Minor syllables of sesquisyllables and syllabic nasals are not counted (pp.199-200); reduction of a full syllable to a minor syllable can make stress appear antepenultimate, e.g. /n1gaa1 sum3mun3/ 'dust' stressed on /gaa1/ (p.200); in serial-verb/verb-complex constructions the last lexical/modifying verb before the final particle carries the phrasal stress and light verbs are unstressed (pp.200-201, sec. 10.8); a stressed allomorph of the realis particle exists (p.153).
new_statements.domain_note: Author explicitly treats stress as phrase-level (penultimate major syllable of the phrase), demonstrated on citation-form compounds ('toe', 'kettle', 'earth/land', 'dust'), noun+DEF phrases and clause-final verb complexes from texts, with F0 and amplitude measurements from one main consultant (Kon Kham Turung). Word-level prosody is iambic (unstressed minor + full major syllable). Language is tonal (3 tones), and tone contrasts are partly neutralised by phrasal position (Table 67, p.199).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: IDENTITY MISMATCH -- READ BEFORE FILING. Glottolog turu1249 'Turung' is classified Tai-Kadai > Southwestern Tai > Sukaphic: that is the historical Tai variety ('Tairong'), whose only linguistic record is Grierson 1904:167-170 (silent on tones and accent) and which Morey 2005:29-31 declares extinct as a Tai language. The ~1,200 Turung people of Jorhat/Golaghat/Karbi Anglong (the population behind the Ethnologue [try] entry that Glottolog's AES status cites) speak a variety of Singpho/Jinghpaw (Tibeto-Burman, Sal > Jingpho), and THAT is the language described by Morey 2010 (quoted here) and Gogoi 2024 ('They speak a variant of Singpho (ISO 639-3: sgp) that incorporates Tai words', ch.4 p.149). Glottolog itself files Morey 2010 under language code 'Singpho (Turung) [sgp]' = sing1264 Northern Jinghpaw (glottolog-cldf 5.1 sources.bib ref 11804), not under turu1249. If this statement enters the catalog it must carry family = Sino-Tibetan (Jinghpaw), ideally keyed as the Turung variety of sing1264; filing it under turu1249 with family Tai-Kadai would put a Tibeto-Burman prosodic system into the Tai-Kadai counts. For turu1249 sensu stricto (Tai Turung) the honest status is 'accessible description silent on stress / no phonology recoverable' (Grierson 1904: 'Tones. -- I regret that I can give no information on this subject').

sources.note: Ch.3 sec. 3.1.4 p.84: stress 'is a phrase level phenomenon'; 'at the phrase level, stress appears to fall on the penultimate syllable, provided that syllable is not a minor syllable'. Ch.5 sec. 5.3 'Phrase internal stress' pp.199-201: penultimate MAJOR syllable of the phrase (compounds, noun+DEF, verb complexes), minor syllables of sesquisyllables and syllabic nasals not counted; with F0/amplitude evidence; p.98: minor syllable of a sesquisyllable is unstressed and toneless. Three lexical tones (3.1.3, 5.2).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Read contents, abstract, ch.1-4. 'Tai Turung' here = the living Singpho-based variety (ch.4 p.149: 'They speak a variant of Singpho (ISO 639-3: sgp) that incorporates Tai words'; ch.1 pp.10-12: ~1200 speakers, six villages). Phoneme inventory, syllable structure (tautosyllabic and 'sesquisyllabic clusters', sec. 3.4 pp.124-128), three tones after Morey 2010 plus a one-speaker F0 study (sec. 4.3 pp.149-155). No word-stress statement for Turung; the only stress sentences (ch.2 pp.51, 67) describe Inga via Goedemans & van der Hulst.
